title: Women’s Pro Baseball League, The Realest partner on historic trading card deal
content:
We don’t always know the best baseball cards are important right away.

They just sit there. In packs. In binders. In shoe boxes. In the hands of people who like the player before the market decides it should care. Then time passes, the story gets bigger, and suddenly that early card becomes proof someone was paying attention before everyone else caught up.

The Women’s Pro Baseball League does not have that kind of cardboard history yet. It doesn’t have decades of flagship sets or annual checklist complaints or oddball releases waiting in dollar boxes. The league has not played its first game, but through a new partnership with The Realest, it is already creating its first official card record.

For collectors, the interesting part is that the WPBL and The Realest are documenting the beginning as it happens.

The WPBL will debut Aug. 1 at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield, Ill., with four teams representing Boston, Los Angeles, New York and San Francisco. The Realest, founded by Scott Keeney, better known as DJ Skee, will create what the company and the league describe as the first officially licensed, league-wide trading card program for an active women’s professional baseball league in the United States.

The cards are expected to include historical photos, action images from the league’s first games and relic cards using authenticated game-used equipment. The Realest will also serve as the league’s official memorabilia authentication partner, using its TRuEST witness-based verification system to authenticate baseballs, jerseys, lineup cards, field dirt, patches and other items.

Details such as checklist size, release format, pricing and distribution for the cards have not yet been announced.

Starting from scratch gives the WPBL some room most card products do not get. It does not have to inherit the hobby’s old rules before it even has a box score. The cards can introduce the league, build early fan habits and give collectors something to care about before the market chimes in.

“The way that we’ve approached this is building an end-to-end program that combines trading cards, memorabilia and culture,” Keeney said.

Cards for a new league cannot just look nice and call it a day. They have to introduce players, teach fans the teams and give people a physical reason to care before there are years of stats, rivalries and local habits doing the work.

When asked why trading cards became part of the league’s launch plan, WPBL commissioner and co-founder Justine Siegal’s answer was immediate.

“Well, I can’t imagine having a league and not having a trading card,” Siegal said. “I mean, it’s baseball. They’re synonymous. Baseball cards and baseball.”

It sounds obvious. It has not always been treated that way. Women have played baseball for generations, but they have rarely been granted the obvious parts of baseball culture: cards, jerseys of their own, memorabilia and real-time archives.

Siegal’s own baseball history runs through a lot of firsts: She was the first woman to coach a professional men’s baseball team (the Brockton Rox in the independent Canadian American Association of Professional Baseball), throw batting practice for an MLB team (Cleveland Guardians) and coach in an MLB organization (Athletics).

The WPBL is new. Women’s baseball is not. That distinction matters.

The Opening Day patches may carry more weight than a square of fabric should. They will be worn on field, removed, authenticated and eventually used in collectible products. What should those patches represent? The question made Siegal laugh.

“I laughed because everything,” Siegal said. “It’s my entire life’s work.

She talked about the 70 years since the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League and about being 13, when she was told she should quit baseball because she was a girl. Now, a young fan can soon hold a card with a patch worn by a WPBL player who pushed through some of those same barriers.

“To me, it’s everything,” Siegal said.

For collectors, some of the best cards not only show who played, but they also explain why a moment mattered. Why someone saved the jersey. Why a patch became worth putting into a card instead of sitting in a storage bin.

The WPBL has the chance to build those connections early because the cards are part of the league’s first season infrastructure. The Realest and the league have room to think about access, history and fan connection before the market tells everyone what the “right” chase names are supposed to be.

Keeney said accessibility is part of the plan.

“Access is always super important,” he said. “We also don’t want to be exclusive.”

He acknowledged the appeal of high-end sales and chase pieces, but said The Realest is trying to keep the first card set simple, while offering a wider range of memorabilia. Premium, but not closed off.

“We don’t want this to just become a chase and a money product,” Keeney said. “We really want to build the brand and get these in the hands of fans.”

The first WPBL release has to serve serious collectors without making new fans feel like they showed up too late. A new league needs the kid buying her first card and the baseball fan who learns one player, then another, then suddenly has a team.

Authentication is the place where The Realest may be able to give the product a clearer hobby identity. Relic cards can be wonderful. A piece of a jersey can feel magical. It can also feel unremarkable when collectors have no real sense of where the material came from or why it matters.

Keeney said WPBL relics will be supported by The Realest’s on-site authentication and scannable records.

“We’ll be able to give you all the information,” he said. “The way that our authentication works is it serves as a living archive.”

For women’s baseball, a living archive is the point. Too much of the sport’s history has required people to hunt for evidence after the fact. Photos, jerseys, scorecards, names, stories. The Realest is trying to make sure first-season WPBL objects enter the record as they happen.

Siegal said one element she particularly values is that The Realest will authenticate players’ own gear, too. A first jersey. Catcher’s gear. Something a player can keep, display, hand down or sell later with its history attached.

“In many ways, I have the intangible that needs to last forever,” Siegal said. “And Skee has the tangible.”

The line gets at why the partnership could be a meaningful one. Siegal is building the pathway. The Realest is building the objects that will help people remember what the pathway looked like when it first opened.

Keeney said the card designs are meant to feel vintage and historical while still belonging in 2026. The preview card he showed referenced the 1981 Topps Basketball design, a three-person layout and perforated edges. Collectors will get the reference. New fans will just see a cool card.

Several players are expected to headline the inaugural season, including No. 1 overall draft pick Kelsie Whitmore, plus Mo’ne Davis, Ashton Lansdell, Ayami Sato and Alli Schroder. Those names will get attention. The cards can also help collectors learn the whole league before the first season is even finished.

Keeney said there is pressure to get that right. “We feel a real duty to preserve and to accurately storytell this,” he said. “We can’t create a second-rate product. We can’t create a second-tier experience. We have to execute.”

The WPBL does not have 75 years of cardboard history behind it. That may be the advantage.

The first patch, the first lineup card, the first jersey, the first card pulled by a kid who has been waiting to see women’s baseball treated this way. None of it has to be found later.

It can start saving everything now.
